en: The all-pervading Viśva has outward consciousness; Taijasa, however, has inward consciousness;
and likewise Prājña has dense (unified) consciousness. Thus, the one alone is traditionally taught to be threefold.
Viśva is situated in the right eye; Taijasa is within the mind;
and Prājña is in the space of the heart. Thus, he is established in a threefold manner within the body.
For the Viśva always experiences gross objects, the Taijasa experiences subtle objects, and likewise the Prājña experiences bliss; understand thus the threefold nature of experience. (MandU 1.3)
The gross [state] satisfies the universe, while the subtle [state] satisfies the Taijasa;
likewise, bliss satisfies the Prājña—understand thus the threefold satisfaction.
Whatever is proclaimed as the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer within the three abodes—
he who knows both of these is not defiled while enjoying.
It is the settled conclusion that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the source of all existing things;
the vital breath generates everything, as does the mind, and the Person (puruṣa) produces them separately like rays.
Some who contemplate creation consider it to be a manifestation or an emanation;
others have conceived of creation as being like a dream or an illusion. (MandUkK 1.7)
Those who are certain about creation hold that the Lord’s creation is by mere will;
those who contemplate time believe that the birth of beings proceeds from time.
Some say that creation is for the sake of enjoyment, while others say it is for the sake of sport;
this is the very nature of the Divine, for what desire can there be for one whose wishes are already fulfilled? (MandUkya-Kārikā 1.9)
The Lord who is the master over the cessation of all sufferings, the imperishable,
non-dual with respect to all existents— the gods remember him as the pervasive Fourth (turya).
The Viśva and Taijasa are held to be bound by both cause and effect;
the Prājña is bound by the cause alone; but these two do not exist in the Fourth (turya).
The wise one perceives nothing at all—neither self nor others, neither truth nor even falsehood; that fourth state is ever the seer of all.

The non-apprehension of duality is equal for both the state of deep sleep (prājña) and the fourth state (turya); however, while deep sleep is accompanied by the seed-sleep [of latent impressions], that is not found in the fourth state.
The first two [states] are associated with dreaming and sleep; the wise one (prājña), however, is characterized by the absence of both dream and sleep.
In the fourth state (turya), they certainly perceive neither sleep nor dream.
For one who perceives otherwise, it is a dream; for one who does not know the reality, it is sleep.
When the error regarding these two has perished, one attains the fourth state.
When the individual soul, sleeping through beginningless illusion, awakens,
it then realizes the non-dual reality— unborn, sleepless, and dreamless.
If conceptual proliferation (prapañca) existed, it would undoubtedly cease;
this duality is mere illusion (māyāmātra), for in the ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ) there is non-duality (advaita).
If that which is imagined were to be turned back by someone, this teaching would be for the sake of instruction; once [reality] is known, duality does not exist. (MandUkK 1.18)
When there is no intention to express the "all" (viśva), the excellence of the initial generality [of the letter A] occurs;
and when there is no comprehension of the measure (mātrā), there would indeed be the generality of attainment (āpti).
In the case of the Taijasa state, a clear excellence of consciousness is observed;
likewise, when there is no perception of the objective measures (mātrā), there would be a state of duality of that same kind.
When the wise one is in the state of the syllable *ma*, there is the mental state called *utkaṭa*;
but when there is no perception of the measure (*mātrā*), there is indeed the state of *laya*.
He who, being certain, knows that which is equal and common in the three abodes—
that great sage is worthy of worship by all beings and indeed to be revered.
The letter *A* leads to the Universal (Viśva), the letter *U* likewise to the Radiant (Taijasa), and the letter *M* further to the Cognizant (Prājña); beyond these, there is no further destination.
One should know the syllable *oṃ* part by part; the parts are the measures (*mātrā*), of this there is no doubt.
Having known the syllable *oṃ* part by part, one should not think of anything at all. (MandUkK 1.24)
One should yoke the mind to the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* is the fearless Brahman.
For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, no fear exists anywhere. (MandUkK 1.25)
The syllable Om is indeed the lower Brahman, and the syllable Om is also remembered as the higher.
The syllable Om is without prior, without interior, without exterior, without posterior, and is imperishable.
For the *praṇava* is indeed the beginning of everything, as well as its middle and its end;
having thus known the *praṇava*, one immediately attains that [Brahman]. (MandU 1.27)
One should know the Praṇava as the Lord, residing in the heart of all;
having realized the all-pervading Oṃkāra, the wise man does not grieve.
He by whom the syllable Om is known—that which is measureless, infinite in measure, the cessation of duality, and auspicious—is a sage and a leader of people. (MandU 1.29)
The wise say that all things are unreal in a dream, because those things exist within [the self] and because they are enclosed. (MandU 2.1)
And because the duration of time is not long, he does not see any regions after having gone;
and once awakened, that entire region is no longer found.
And the non-existence of chariots and so forth is heard in accordance with reason; therefore, their unreality is established, for it is said that they are manifested in a dream. (MandUkK 2.3)
But because of their intermediate state, the distinctions [of objects] are known to exist in the waking state;
as it is there, so too in the dream state, they are distinguished by being concealed.
For the wise declare that the states of dreaming and waking are one and the same,
by reason of the very fact that the distinctions between them are equally established.
That which does not exist in the beginning and at the end is likewise so in the present;
though they are similar to the unreal, they are perceived as if they were real.
The fact that these [dream objects] serve a purpose is contradicted by the dream state itself;
therefore, they are indeed remembered as being false, like things at the beginning and the end.
For this is an unprecedented state, like that of the inhabitants of heaven;
having gone there, he perceives them just as one well-trained here [perceives objects].

Even in the state of dreaming, that which is imagined internally by the mind is unreal, while that which is grasped externally by the mind is seen as real; thus, the unreality of these two is observed.
Even during the waking state, that which is imagined internally by the mind is unreal, while that which is grasped externally by the mind is real; thus, the unreality of these two is logical.
If there is the unreality of both [the dream and the waking states] and their various distinctions,
then who perceives these distinctions, and who indeed is the conceptualizer of them?
The divine Self, by its own creative power (māyā), fashions itself as the self;
it is that very same [Self] which perceives the distinctions—such is the certainty of the Vedānta. (MandUpK 2.12)
The Lord transforms other states that are established within the mind, and likewise, he fashions those that are fixed externally; thus does the master conceptualize.

Those things which exist internally as moments of consciousness and those which exist externally as pairs of moments—all of these are merely imagined; their distinction is not caused by anything else.
Those things which are indeed unmanifest within, yet manifest without, are all merely imagined; the difference, however, lies in the variety of the senses.
First, the living being (jīva) imagines speech and various kinds of external and internal entities, according to its ignorance and according to its memory. (MandU 2.16)
Just as a rope, when not clearly discerned in the darkness,
is imagined to be a snake, a stream of water, or other such things, so too is the Self imagined.
Just as when a rope has been definitively determined, conceptual construction ceases and there remains only the non-duality of "it is just a rope," so too is the definitive realization of the Self.
This is the illusion (māyā) of that God, by which he himself is deluded, through which he is conceptualized by means of these infinite entities such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth.
Those who know it as the vital breath (prāṇa) call it so; those who know it as the elements (bhūta) call it so;
those who know it as the qualities (guṇa) call it so; and those who know it as the principles (tattva) call it so. (MandU 2.20)
Those who know the quarters say they are the quarters; those who know the objects say they are the objects;
those who know the worlds say they are the worlds; and those who know the gods say they are the gods. (MandU 2.21)

Those who know the Vedas say, "The Vedas"; those who know sacrifice say, "Sacrifice"; those who know the enjoyer say, "The enjoyer"; and those who know the object of enjoyment say, "The object of enjoyment. (MandU 2.22)

"It is subtle," say those who know it as subtle; "it is gross," say those who know it as gross. "It is embodied," say those who know it as embodied; "it is formless," say those who know it as formless. (MandU 2.23)
Those who know time call it "time"; those who know the quarters call them "quarters";
those who know arguments call them "arguments"; and those who know the worlds call them "worlds. (MandU 2.24)

Those who know it as the mind call it *manas*; those who know it as the intellect call it *buddhi*; those who know it as the heart call it *citta*; and those who know it as such call it merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). (MandUkK 2.25)
Some say it consists of twenty-five principles, others of twenty-six;
some say it consists of thirty-one, and others that it is infinite. (MandUkK 2.26)

Those who know the worlds call them "stages of life" (āśramas); those who know that [reality] call them "genders"—feminine, masculine, and neuter—while others call them "the higher and the lower. (MandUk 2.27)
Those who know creation call it "creation"; those who know dissolution call it "dissolution";
and those who know persistence call it "persistence"—yet all of these are always [identical] here in this world.
Whatever state he shows to another, that state indeed the other perceives;
having become that very thing, he protects him, and that grasping at it approaches him.
By these non-distinct states, this [Self] is characterized as if it were distinct;
he who knows this according to reality may form such a conception without hesitation. (MandU 2.30)
Just as a dream and an illusion are seen, and just as a city of the Gandharvas is seen,
so too is this entire universe seen by the wise in the Vedāntas.
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one bound nor a practitioner,
neither one desiring liberation nor indeed one liberated— this is the ultimate truth.
This [world] is imagined through non-dual means by means of entities that are themselves non-existent;
and entities too are [imagined] precisely by means of non-duality. Therefore, non-duality is auspicious.
Those who know reality understand that this [world] is not identical with the self, nor is it different from itself in any way; nothing whatsoever is either separate or non-separate. (MandUk 2.34)
For this non-conceptual state, the cessation of proliferation, which is non-dual, has been seen by sages who have transcended passion, fear, and anger, and who have mastered the Vedas.
Therefore, having understood this, one should fix one's mindfulness upon non-duality;
having fully attained non-duality, one should conduct oneself in the world like an insentient being.
Free from praise, free from salutation, and likewise free from the utterance of *svadhā*,
the ascetic, whose dwelling is both moving and unmoving, should live on whatever comes by chance.
Having seen the reality within and having seen the reality without, one becomes that very reality;
delighting therein, one shall not fall away from reality.
The dharma based on ritual worship exists only after Brahman has been born;
since everything was unborn prior to its origination, that [dharma] is considered pitiable.
Therefore, I shall explain that which is free from wretchedness, unborn, and attained to equanimity—
how nothing whatsoever is born, even as it is being born on all sides.
For the Self has arisen as individual souls like space, like the spaces within jars;
and it has arisen through aggregates like the jars themselves—this is the illustration regarding birth. (MandUkK 3.3)
Just as when jars and other such objects have dissolved, the spaces within those jars and so forth merge back into the [great] space,
even so do the individual souls (jīvas) here merge into the Self (ātman).
Just as when the space within one jar is joined with dust, smoke, and so forth,
not all [spaces] are joined [with them], so too are the individual souls [joined] with pleasure and the like.
Indeed, names and functions of form differ here and there;
yet there is no difference in space. Such is the determination regarding individual souls.
Just as the space within a jar is neither a modification nor a part of space,
so too the individual soul (jīva) is never a modification nor a part of the Self (ātman).
Just as the sky appears soiled by impurities to the ignorant,
so too does the self appear soiled by impurities to those lacking wisdom.
In death and in birth, in going and in coming,
and in remaining within all bodies, it is indistinguishable from space.
All composite aggregates are like dreams, projected by the self's own illusory power (māyā);
for no logical justification exists for either their superiority or their total identity [with the self].
For those sheaths beginning with "rasa" which have been explained in the Taittirīyaka,
their Self is the Supreme, the individual soul (jīva), as has been clearly revealed as being like space (kha).
In each pair, through the knowledge of the honey, the Supreme Brahman is revealed—
just as space is revealed in both the earth and the belly.
The non-difference between the individual self (jīva) and the Self (ātman) is praised through their identity; and that manifoldness which is censured—this alone is indeed consistent. (MandUpK 3.13)

The distinctness between the individual self (jīva) and the Self (ātman) that was proclaimed prior to creation is figurative, based on a future state; for its primary sense is not tenable [at that time].

The creation described otherwise by means of clay, iron, sparks, and so forth, is merely a pedagogical device for the sake of instruction; there is no difference whatsoever [between the illustrations and the reality]. (MandU 3.15)
The stages of life (āśramas) are of three kinds, characterized by inferior, middling, and superior views;
this instruction on worship was taught for their sake out of compassion.
Those who maintain dualistic views are firmly convinced of their own established doctrines and contradict one another; by them, however, this [non-dual teaching] is not contradicted.
For non-duality is indeed the ultimate reality, while duality is said to be its differentiation;
since for them there is duality in both ways, this [teaching] is not contradicted by that.
For this [unborn] is divided by illusion (māyā), but not otherwise in any way;
for if it were divided in reality, the immortal would fall into mortality. (MandU 3.19)
The proponents [of arising] desire the birth of an entity that is indeed unborn;
for how can an entity that is unborn and immortal undergo mortality?
The mortal does not become immortal, nor likewise does the immortal become mortal;
a change in the nature of things (prakṛti) will never occur in any way whatsoever.
For one whose inherently immortal being undergoes mortality,
how can that which is produced as immortal remain unshakable?
Whether [the world] is created as real or even as unreal, the scriptural testimony is the same;
that which is certain and endowed with reason is [to be accepted], and nothing else. (MandUkK 3.23)

"From the Vedic revelation, 'Not here, not manifold,' and also from 'Indra by means of his powers of illusion' (māyābhiḥ), it follows that he who is unborn is born in many ways through māyā. (MandU 3.24)
By the denial of origination, arising itself is negated;
by the question "Who indeed could produce this?", the cause is negated.
Since this very [Self] negates everything explained as "not this, not this," it shines forth as unborn by reason of its being ungraspable.
For birth is possible through illusion for one who exists, but not in reality;
for him by whom something is born in reality, that which was already born is born again.
The birth of that which is non-existent is not logically possible even through illusion;
the son of a barren woman is born neither in reality nor even through illusion. (MandUkK 3.28)
Just as in a dream the mind moves with its appearance of duality through illusion,
so too in the waking state the mind moves with its appearance of duality through illusion.
The mind is non-dual yet appears as dual in a dream—of this there is no doubt;
likewise, it is non-dual yet appears as dual in the waking state—of this there is no doubt.
This duality, whatever it may be, including all that is moving and unmoving, is the vision of the mind;
for when the mind becomes non-mind, duality is no longer perceived at all.

When, through the realization of the truth of the Self, one no longer forms conceptual constructions, then one attains the state of mindlessness; for in the absence of an object to be grasped, there is no grasping.
They declare that non-conceptual, unborn knowledge is non-different from the object of knowledge;
the unborn, eternal Brahman, which is the object of knowledge, is realized by the unborn [knower] as being unborn.

The movement of the wise one whose mind has been restrained and is free from conceptual construction should be understood as being like that in deep sleep; it is not otherwise, nor is it equal to anything else.
For in deep sleep it dissolves; when restrained, it does not dissolve.
That itself is the fearless Brahman, the light of knowledge on all sides.
The unborn, without Indra, without sleep, nameless, formless,
ever-luminous, and all-knowing— of this there is no figurative description whatsoever.
Free from all verbal expression, arisen above all thought,
perfectly tranquil, a single light, the samādhi is immovable and fearless.
There is neither grasping nor relinquishing where no thought exists;
then knowledge is established in itself, unborn and attained to equanimity.
The yoga known as "the touchless" is indeed difficult to perceive for all yogis;
for yogis fear it, seeing danger where there is no danger.
For all yogins, freedom from fear, the destruction of suffering, awakening, and indeed imperishable peace depend upon the restraint of the mind.
Just as the ocean might be emptied drop by drop with the tip of a blade of kusha grass,
so too the restraint of the mind occurs through tireless effort.

By means of skillful methods, one should restrain the mind when it is distracted by sensual enjoyments, and likewise when it is overly tranquil or in a state of lethargy; as is desire, so is lethargy.
Recalling that all is suffering, one should turn away from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
by recollecting the unborn, one no longer perceives what is born.
One should uplift the mind when it is sluggish and calm it again when it is distracted;
one should recognize it when it is affected by passion, and once it has attained equanimity, one should not disturb it.
One should not relish the bliss therein; being free from attachment, one should become established through wisdom.
One should strive to unify the mind that is moving outward so that it becomes motionless.
When the mind neither dissolves nor is distracted again,
being unshakable and free from appearances, then that is the perfected Brahman.
They declare the All-Knowing One to be self-abiding, tranquil, possessing nirvāṇa, ineffable, the supreme bliss, unborn, and known through that which is unborn.
No living being is born; its origin does not exist.
This is that supreme truth wherein nothing whatsoever is born.
I pay homage to the Fully Awakened One, the best among bipeds, who, through wisdom like space, perceives all phenomena as being like the sky, and is non-different from that which is to be known.
I bow to that which is called the yoga of non-contact, which is beneficial and brings happiness to all beings, and which is taught as being without dispute and without conflict. (MandUpK 4.2)
For indeed, some disputants maintain that what exists comes into being, while other wise ones, contending with one another, maintain that what does not exist comes into being. (MandUk 4.3)
Nothing that exists is born, nor does anything non-existent ever arise; thus, by disputing [this], they proclaim non-arising as non-dual. (MandU 4.4)
We approve of the non-arising (ajāti) being proclaimed by them;
we do not dispute with them—understand this as non-dispute. (MandUkK 4.5)
The proponents [of birth] desire the birth of a phenomenon that is indeed unborn;
for how can a phenomenon that is unborn and immortal undergo mortality?
The mortal does not become immortal, nor likewise does the immortal become mortal;
a change in the nature of things (prakṛti) will never occur in any way whatsoever.
If one's dharma, which is by nature immortal, undergoes mortality,
how can that which is made immortal by artificial means remain unshakable?
That which is innate, natural, co-emergent, and uncreated—
know that to be *prakṛti* (primordial nature), which does not abandon its own essential being.
All phenomena are by their very nature free from old age and death;
yet, desiring old age and death, they fall away through that mental conception.
If an effect indeed has a cause, then that [cause] becomes a cause;
how can that which is being born be unborn, and how can it be both distinct and eternal? (MandUkK 4.11)
If the effect is non-different from the cause, then the effect would be unborn;
for how, according to you, could the cause be permanent if it arises from the effect that is being born? (MandUk 4.12)
For one for whom the unborn is born, there is indeed no illustrative example;
and if that which is already born were to be born again, an infinite regress would result.
For those for whom the cause has a beginning and the effect has a beginning, how can they describe the cause and the effect as being without beginning? (MandUk 4.14)
For those for whom the cause is the beginning of the effect, and the effect is the beginning of the cause—
such would be their birth, just as the birth of a father comes from a son.
If cause and effect are to arise, their sequence must be sought by you;
for if they were to arise simultaneously, there would be no connection between them, like [the two horns of] a cow.
While the effect is in the process of arising, your cause is not established;
how can an unestablished cause produce an effect?
If the establishment of the cause is from the effect, and the establishment of the effect is from the cause,
which of the two is established first, such that the other is established in dependence upon it?
"Whether due to incapacity, lack of understanding, or else a violation of the proper sequence—in every such way, the Buddhas have elucidated non-arising. (MandUpK 4.19)
The analogy known as the seed and the sprout is always equivalent to the point to be proven;
for a reason that is equivalent to the point to be proven is not suitable for establishing that which is to be proven.
The lack of knowledge regarding what precedes and what follows illuminates non-arising;
for how could that which is currently arising not be perceived as preceding it? (MandUpK 4.21)
No entity whatsoever is born from itself, nor from another, nor from both; no entity whatsoever is born that is existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent.
A cause does not arise from that which is beginningless, nor does an effect [arise] by way of its own nature;
for that which has no beginning truly has no beginning.
The dependent nature is held to exist because designation has a cause, otherwise there would be the destruction of duality, and because affliction is perceived. (MandUpK 4.24)
The state of having signs is accepted for conceptual designation because it is seen through reasoning;
the signlessness of the sign is accepted because it is seen through the vision of reality.
The mind does not touch the object, nor likewise the appearance of the object;
for since the object is unreal, the appearance of the object is not separate from it.
The mind does not always come into contact with signs throughout the three periods of time;
how, then, can there be error for that which is signless?
Therefore, the mind is not born, nor is that which is seen by the mind born;
those who perceive its birth truly perceive a track in the sky.
Since that which is unborn is born, therefore non-birth is its nature;
there can never be any alteration of this nature.
The finitude of a beginningless saṃsāra will not be established;
nor will there be an infinity for a liberation that has a beginning. (MandU 4.30)
That which does not exist in the beginning and at the end likewise does not exist in the present;
though they are similar to the unreal, they are perceived as if they were real.
The fact that they possess a purpose is contradicted by the dream state;
therefore, because they have a beginning and an end, they are indeed remembered as being false.
All phenomena are false, for they are seen as the end of the body within a dream;
when this region has ceased to exist, how indeed can there be a perception of beings?
It is not logical that [the soul] goes to see [the dream objects], because there is no fixed time for such a journey;
moreover, upon waking, none of those [objects] are found in that place.
Having deliberated with friends and others, one does not find anything upon awakening;
nor does one perceive anything whatsoever that was previously grasped. (MandUk 4.35)
In a dream, the body is unreal because it is seen as something distinct from oneself;
as is the body, so too everything perceived by the mind is unreal.
Because of the grasping [of objects], dream is held to have the waking state as its cause;
yet because it is the cause of that very [waking state], the waking state is held to belong to that [dream] alone.
Because arising is not established, everything is declared to be unborn;
nor is there any possibility whatsoever for that which has not come into being to arise from that which has already come into being.
Having seen what is unreal while awake, one sees it in a dream, being absorbed in that;
and having seen it even in an unreal dream, one does not see it upon waking.
There is no non-existent thing that has a non-existent cause, nor likewise one that has both existent and non-existent causes;
there is no existent thing that has an existent cause, so how could there be a non-existent thing that has an existent cause?
Just as one might perceive unthinkable things as real due to a cognitive distortion while awake,
so too does one see phenomena right there in a dream due to a cognitive distortion.
For those who maintain that things exist because they are perceived and because of conventional practice,
the Buddhas have taught "birth" (jāti) merely as a means for those who are constantly terrified of "non-birth" (ajāti).
For those who tremble at the unborn because they perceive [existence], their faults arising from birth will not be established; even if there is a fault, it will be slight.

Just as a "phantom elephant" is spoken of because it is perceived and because of its conventional behavior, so too is a real entity said to exist because it is perceived and because of its conventional behavior. (MandUk 4.44)
Manifesting as birth, manifesting as movement, and likewise manifesting as an object—consciousness is in fact unborn, motionless, and without objective reality; it is peaceful and non-dual.
In this way the mind is not born; in this way all phenomena are known to be unborn.
Those who understand it thus do not fall into error.
Just as the flickering of a firebrand appears as straight, curved, and so forth,
so too does the vibration of consciousness appear as the perceived object and the perceiving subject.
Just as a firebrand that does not move is without appearance, unborn, and unchanging,
so too consciousness that does not move is without appearance, unborn, and unchanging.
When a firebrand is whirled, the appearances do not come from elsewhere;
nor do they, being motionless, enter the firebrand from anywhere other than that.
They have not emerged from the firebrand, because they lack the nature of a substantial entity;
the same would apply to consciousness as well, since there is no difference in their appearance.
When consciousness is indeed vibrating, appearances do not come from elsewhere;
nor do they enter into consciousness from anywhere else, for they are not distinct from it, nor are they motionless.
They do not emerge from consciousness, because they lack substantiality;
since they are always inconceivable, they possess neither the nature of cause nor effect.
For one substance could indeed be the cause of another substance, and likewise one thing of another;
however, neither substantiality nor the state of being something else is possible for dharmas.
Thus, phenomena are not born from the mind, nor is the mind born from phenomena;
in this way, the wise enter into the non-arising of cause and effect.
As long as there is the penetration of cause and effect, so long does the arising of cause and effect continue;
when the penetration of cause and effect has ceased, there is no further arising of cause and effect.
As long as there is the penetration of cause and effect, so long is saṃsāra extended;
when the penetration of cause and effect is exhausted, one does not enter into saṃsāra.
Everything arises through conventional reality; therefore, indeed, there is no eternalism.
For everything is unborn in its true being; therefore, indeed, there is no nihilism.
Those phenomena which are said to arise do not arise in reality;
their birth is like an illusion, and that illusion does not exist.
Just as from a seed consisting of illusion a sprout consisting of that same illusion arises— neither eternal nor subject to annihilation— such is the application [of this principle] to all phenomena.
In all phenomena, which are beyond being born, there is no designation of "eternal" or "non-eternal";
where letters do not function, there distinction is not expressed.
Just as in a dream the mind moves through illusion with the appearance of duality,
so too in the waking state the mind moves through illusion with the appearance of duality.
The mind is non-dual yet appears as dual in a dream, there is no doubt;
likewise, it is non-dual yet appears as dual in the waking state, there is no doubt. (MandUkK 4.62)
The dreamer, moving about in a dream, always sees those living beings— whether born from eggs or born from sweat— who are situated throughout the ten directions.
Those objects perceived by the mind of the dreamer do not exist apart from it;
likewise, this very object of perception is held to be the mind of the dreamer itself.
While wandering awake during his waking state, he constantly beholds those living beings— whether born from eggs or born from sweat— who reside in the ten directions.
Those [objects] are not found to exist apart from the waking consciousness that perceives them;
likewise, this very visible world is held to be the waking mind itself.
For both of these are mutually perceived; how can it be said that "that exists"?
In that view, both are devoid of defining characteristics and are not grasped at all.
Just as a living being consisting of a dream is born and also dies,
so too all these living beings come into existence and cease to exist.
Just as a life-spirit consisting of illusion is born and also dies,
so too all these living beings come into being and cease to be.
Just as a magically created being is born and also dies,
so too all these living beings come into existence and cease to exist.
No living being is born; its origin does not exist.
This is that supreme truth wherein nothing whatsoever is born.
This duality, appearing as the grasped and the grasper, is merely the vibration of the mind;
therefore, the mind is proclaimed to be eternally without object and unattached.
That which exists by way of imagined convention does not exist in the ultimate sense;
that which exists by way of dependent convention may exist, but it does not exist from the perspective of the ultimate truth.
The unborn is so by means of imagined convention, but in the ultimate sense it is not even unborn;
however, through the perfection of the dependent nature and so forth, it is born by way of convention.
There is an adherence to what is unreal; therein duality does not exist.
Having realized the absence of duality, one becomes signless and is no longer born.
When one does not find causes—whether superior, inferior, or middling—then the mind is not born; in the absence of a cause, how can there be a fruit?
The non-arising of the signless mind is equanimous and non-dual,
because all that is seen by the mind is indeed unborn.
Having realized that the state of being a causal sign is real, and no longer apprehending it as a separate cause,
one attains the state that is free from sorrow, likewise free from desire, and fearless.
For due to adherence to what is unreal, that [cognition] proceeds with respect to what appears similar;
but upon realizing the non-existence of the object, it turns back without attachment.
For the state of one who has desisted and does not engage [with objects] is indeed motionless;
that is the domain of the Buddhas, for it is that equanimity which is unborn and non-dual.
Unborn, sleepless, and dreamless, it is itself ever-luminous;
for this reality is once and for all radiant by its very nature as the *dharmadhātu*.
By the grasping of any dharma whatsoever, that Blessed One is constantly veiled by happiness and perpetually unveiled by suffering.

"It exists," "it does not exist," "it both exists and does not exist," or again, "it neither exists nor does not exist"—the fool thus obscures [reality] through notions of movement, stability, both, or neither. (MandUk 4.83)
These are the four quarters which are always occupied by the planets;
he by whom the Blessed One is seen as untouched by these is all-seeing.
Having attained complete omniscience, the state of Brahmanhood which is non-dual and devoid of beginning,
middle, or end— what more could one possibly strive for beyond this?
For this discipline of the wise is called ordinary tranquility;
self-restraint arises from the natural state of being already restrained. Thus, the man of knowledge should attain tranquility.
That which possesses an object and is accompanied by perception is held to be mundane duality;
that which lacks an object but is accompanied by perception is held to be pure mundane [wisdom].

Non-existence and non-apprehension are remembered as supramundane; this is proclaimed by the Buddhas as that which is to be known, the object of knowledge, and that which is to be fully realized. (MandUpK 4.88)

When the threefold knowledge and the object of knowledge have been understood in their proper sequence by oneself, omniscience indeed arises everywhere for the one of great intelligence in this world. (MandUpK 4.89)
That which is to be abandoned, that which is to be known, that which is to be attained, and that which is to be purified are to be understood according to the supreme path.
Among these, it is taught that perception occurs in three, excluding that which is to be known.
By their very nature, all phenomena are to be known as beginningless like space;
for in them there exists no diversity whatsoever anywhere.
All phenomena are by their very nature primordially awakened and perfectly certain;
he who possesses such patient acceptance is fit for immortality.
For all phenomena are primordially quiescent, unarisen, and by their very nature perfectly extinguished; they are all equal and undifferentiated—the unborn, the equanimous, and the fearless.
But for those who always wander in duality, there is indeed no fearlessness;
they are inclined toward division and speak of difference, and therefore they are considered wretched.
But those who, in this present age, shall become firmly resolved upon equanimity— they indeed possess great wisdom in this world, yet the world does not penetrate that [truth].
Knowledge is held to be unborn and non-transmigrating with respect to phenomena that are themselves unborn;
because knowledge does not proceed [toward them], it is therefore proclaimed to be unattached.
When even the slightest difference arises for one who lacks wisdom, there is never any non-attachment; how much less, then, the falling away of obscurations?
All phenomena are unobstructed and pure by nature;
they were enlightened from the beginning and thus liberated—such is the realization of the Leaders.
The knowledge of the Buddha, the Protector, does not proceed toward phenomena;
all phenomena are likewise [non-proceeding], and this was not spoken by the Buddha. (MandUpK 4.99)
Having realized the state that is difficult to perceive, profoundly deep, unborn, equanimous, confident, and without diversity, we pay homage according to our strength.
